newsitem.title: FRANCE: Socialists trumpet Mobutu ouster as French defeat.
newsitem.headline: Socialists trumpet Mobutu ouster as French defeat.

text.p: France's Socialist opposition has pounced on the ousting of Zaire's president Mobutu Sese Seko as a failure for President Jacques Chirac's Africa policy, a week before a French parliamentary election.

But neither major party can claim the moral high ground in France's complex relations with its former African colonies and former Belgian colonies such as Zaire, and political analysts said the issue is unlikely to influence voters.

One French analyst said the fall of Mobutu could have a domino effect on French-backed governments in neighbouring Congo and the Central African Republic, where Paris has its biggest military base on the continent.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin accused the centre-right government of having renewed French support for Mobutu after other Western countries had ostracised him for his record on corruption and human rights.

"This affair seals the bankruptcy of France's Africa policy. The present government was wrong to have put president Mobutu back in the saddle after we had tried, albeit rather late, to distance ourselves from him," Jospin said.

The rout of Mobutu by rebels led by the English-speaking Laurent Kabila, backed by Uganda and Rwanda, is widely seen as a defeat for French influence on the continent it has long regarded as its backyard, and a sign of growing U.S. influence -- even though Mobutu was first backed and financed by the United States and long supported by other Western powers.

U.S. officials insist there is no deliberate drive to diminish French influence in Africa. But they say the end of the Cold War means corrupt, anti-communist strongmen should no longer count on Western support.

Diplomats date the start of the French decline to the fall of a French-backed Hutu-led government in Rwanda in 1994, driven out by Ugandan-backed Tutsi rebels after Hutu extremists massacred hundreds of thousands of Tutsis.
Many of the Hutu militiamen found sanctuary in Zaire amid a flow of refugees protected by French troops in an "Operation Turquoise" relief operation.

"Ever since its debacle in Rwanda, Paris has constantly been on the defensive, its Africa policy reduced to a vain attempt to escape new condemnations," said Stephen Smith, Africa expert of the Paris daily Liberation.

"At least two former colonies, Zaire's neighbours Congo and the Central African Republic, could topple in the coming months even without outside destabilisation, providing further proof of the demise of 'Pax Franca' in the tropics," he wrote.
In the last few weeks, Paris and Washington worked together in vain to arrange a negotiated transfer of power in Zaire.
French officials said the Americans seemed belatedly worried that Kabila might be no less ruthless a strongman than Mobutu.

Nevertheless, France looks like the biggest loser in Zaire because it stuck longest, and most publicly, to Mobutu, declaring him to be "essential" to any solution long after his ouster seemed only a matter of time.

When other countries, even neutral Switzerland, closed their doors to him, France allowed the veteran ruler in the trademark leopard-skin hat to stay in his French Riviera villa while undergoing cancer treatment in Monaco.

Diplomats said that was Chirac's personal choice. But it undermined the credibility of French calls for international humanitarian action to save Rwandan refugees in rebel-held eastern Zaire and appeals for elections in Zaire.
Ironically, France never had major economic interests in Africa's third-largest state, whose mineral wealth American, South African and Canadian firms have rushed to exploit.

Annual trade with Kinshasa was worth a paltry 350 million francs ($60 million). France's interest in the sprawling giant spanning from the Great Lakes of central Africa to the Atlantic was political and strategic.
As the natural leader and main aid donor of the community of French-speaking states, Paris has long sought to maintain an African commonwealth sharing its language and culture.
In some of those states, notably Ivory Coast and Gabon, it has important economic interests. In others, such as Zaire, there is a large French-speaking population.
